oneSentence: Using computing services over a network from remote data centres, instead of owning and running all the machines yourself.
plainExplanation:
Cloud computing means renting computing services over the internet or another network. Those services can include storage, databases, software, and processing power. Processing power means the machine resources used to run programs, such as memory and chips.

What goes in can be your files, your software, or a request to run a task. For example, you might upload a document, send data to be analysed, or ask an application to translate text. The request travels to remote servers, which are computers in large data centres run by a provider.

What happens next is that the provider’s systems store the data, run the software, and send back a result. You do not usually see the physical machines. You mainly choose what service you need, how much you need, and who is allowed to access it.

What comes out can be a saved file, a web app, an API response, or a completed computation. The main benefit is flexibility: you can start quickly and increase or reduce usage without buying new hardware. But cloud computing is not just “someone else’s computer”. That phrase is useful, but too simple. The details of security, location, cost, reliability, and legal control still matter.

everydayAnalogy.title: Using a shared translation office
everydayAnalogy.story: A small team in Nairobi needs a short field report translated into French today. Instead of hiring full-time translators for every language, they send the text to a trusted translation service centre that already has staff, desks, dictionaries, and workflow tools. The centre does the work and sends the translated report back quickly. If ten more reports arrive tomorrow, the team can ask for more help without building a bigger office first.

mapping.aiElement: cloud provider running remote servers and services
sending data or a request over a network
shared computing resources such as storage, software, and processors
processed output returned to the user

everydayAnalogy.limitation: A translation office uses people, while cloud computing mainly uses automated systems running on machines. Also, cloud services are not always as simple as handing work to one centre: data may be copied across regions, split across many servers, or controlled by contracts and technical settings. The analogy helps with the idea of renting capacity, but it does not explain networking, security controls, or data location well.

visual.title: How cloud computing works in practice
visual.learningObjective: After viewing this diagram, a reader should be able to explain how a user request goes to remote computing resources and returns as a result, and why this differs from running everything on one local machine.
visual.description: A left-to-right flow with four boxes connected by arrows. It shows a user device sending a task through a network to a cloud provider, where remote servers store or process it, then returning the result. Read from left to right.

steps.label: 1. User starts a task
steps.explanation: A person uses a laptop or phone to store a file, open an app, or request a computation.
steps.visualInstruction: Draw a laptop and phone in the first box with short labels: file, app, task.

steps.label: 2. Request travels over a network
steps.explanation: The task and any needed data are sent over the internet or another approved network connection.
steps.visualInstruction: Draw arrows from devices to a cloud icon or network line in the second box.

steps.label: 3. Remote systems handle the work
steps.explanation: Servers in a provider’s data centre store data, run software, or process the request using shared resources.
steps.visualInstruction: Show stacked server racks in the third box with three small tags: storage, software, compute.

steps.label: 4. Result comes back
steps.explanation: The completed file, answer, or service response is returned to the user’s device.
steps.visualInstruction: Draw an arrow back to a screen in the fourth box showing a completed document or status tick.

visual.interaction: Hover or tap each step to reveal a one-sentence note about what goes in, what happens, and what comes out.
visual.accessibilityDescription: The diagram is a four-step flow read from left to right. Step 1 shows a user on a laptop or phone starting a task such as saving a file, opening software, or requesting a translation. Step 2 shows that request moving over a network connection. Step 3 shows remote servers in a provider data centre handling the work, labelled storage, software, and compute. Step 4 shows the result returning to the user’s device as a finished file, response, or running service. The main message is that the computing work happens on remote infrastructure rather than only on the user’s own machine.
visual.reducedMotionDescription: A static four-box flow replaces any animation. Arrows remain fixed, and each box contains its label and explanation in visible text.

workedExample.scenario: A small charity needs to translate and store 25 short reports this week without buying its own server.
workedExample.input: 25 text files, each about 400 words, uploaded from staff laptops to a cloud-based translation and storage service.
process: Staff upload the text files through a web app using their organisation account.
The service sends the files to remote servers that run the translation software and save the originals.
The provider’s systems process the files and create French versions in the same shared workspace.
Staff download the translated files and share links with approved colleagues instead of emailing large attachments.
workedExample.result: By the end of the day, the team has 25 translated files stored online and accessible to authorised staff, without setting up or maintaining its own server.

unWorkplaceExample.scenario: A country office uses a cloud-based email and workflow system to help triage a shared inbox for general public enquiries.
unWorkplaceExample.relevance: Cloud computing lets the office use shared software, storage, and processing without running its own mail servers locally, which can improve continuity and access across locations.
unWorkplaceExample.caution: Only approved organisational systems should be used. Staff should not place confidential, personal, protection-sensitive, security-sensitive, or operational information into an unapproved public AI or cloud service.

whyItMatters:
Cloud computing affects cost, speed, risk, and control. A team can launch services faster because it rents infrastructure instead of buying and maintaining every machine. That can help with scaling up during busy periods and scaling down when demand falls.

But convenience can hide important choices. Where the data is stored may affect legal obligations and data sovereignty. How the service is configured affects security, access control, backup, and reliability. Pricing can look simple at first but grow with heavy use, storage, or data transfer.

For non-specialists, the key decision is not only “cloud or not”. It is which service, for which data, under which rules, with what oversight, and at what total cost.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: The cloud means data floats around with no physical location.
commonMisconceptions.correction: Cloud services still run on physical machines in real data centres. The provider manages them, but location still matters for law, security, latency, and data governance.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Using the cloud is always cheaper.
commonMisconceptions.correction: It can reduce upfront hardware costs, especially for small or changing workloads. But ongoing charges for storage, computing time, users, and data transfer can become high if services are not planned and monitored.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Cloud computing and AI are the same thing.
commonMisconceptions.correction: They are different. Cloud computing is a way to provide computing resources over a network. AI may use cloud resources, but many cloud services have nothing to do with AI, and some AI runs outside the cloud.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: If a provider is reputable, security is fully the provider’s job.
commonMisconceptions.correction: Providers handle some parts, such as operating the infrastructure, but organisations still need to manage their own accounts, permissions, settings, and safe use. Responsibility is shared, not transferred completely.

simpleVsTechnical.simple: Instead of buying and running all your own computers, you rent computing services from a provider over a network and use them when needed.
simpleVsTechnical.technical: Cloud computing is an on-demand delivery model for remote infrastructure and software services over a network. A provider operates data centres and exposes resources such as virtual machines, storage, databases, and managed applications. Users send requests from client devices; the provider authenticates access, allocates compute, stores or processes data, and returns outputs. Key properties often include pooled resources, elastic scaling, measured usage, and remote administration. The term is commonly confused with model hosting, but model hosting is one specific use of cloud or other infrastructure. It is also commonly confused with edge AI, which moves some processing closer to where data is produced rather than relying mainly on central remote servers.

keyTakeaway: Cloud computing lets you rent remote computing capacity quickly, but you still need to manage cost, security, access, and data location carefully.

quickCheck.question: Which description best matches cloud computing?
options: Using remote computing services over a network instead of running everything on your own machines
Any software that uses artificial intelligence to answer questions
Saving files only on the hard drive inside your own laptop
A guarantee that data never leaves your country
quickCheck.explanation: Cloud computing is about where computing resources are provided and managed: remote services over a network. It does not automatically mean AI, local-only storage, or a specific data location.
